title: Implementing Machine Learning Methods in Estimating the Size of the Non-observed Economy
short_title: Machine Learning for Estimating the Size of the Non-observed Economy

affiliations.1: Department of Economics, Western Galilee College, Acre, Israel

abstract: Even though the literature on unregistered economic activity is growing at an increasing rate, we commonly encounter simple ordinary least squares methods and panel regressions, largely ignoring the recent rapid developments in machine learning methods. This study provides a new approach to more accurately estimate the size of the non-observed economy using machine learning methods. Compared to two currency demand-based models used to estimate the size of the non-observed economy, we show that a Random Forest algorithm can more accurately estimate the demand for currency, which is known to provide a fair estimation of the unregistered economic activity. The proposed approach shows superior forecasting capabilities compared to the current state-of-the-art linear regression-based methods dedicated to estimating non-observed economic activity.
summary: The non-observed economy, meaning unregistered economic activity, is usually estimated with simple regression methods that ignore recent advances in machine learning. We propose a machine learning approach in which a Random Forest algorithm estimates the demand for currency, which is known to give a fair estimate of unregistered activity. Compared with two currency demand-based models, the Random Forest estimated currency demand more accurately and forecast better than state-of-the-art linear regression-based methods.
key_findings: Existing studies of unregistered economic activity commonly rely on ordinary least squares and panel regressions, largely ignoring recent machine learning developments.
A Random Forest algorithm estimated the demand for currency more accurately than two currency demand-based models.
The approach showed superior forecasting capabilities compared with state-of-the-art linear regression-based methods for estimating non-observed economic activity.
